summary: "Paul says Genesis spoke of one ‘offspring,’ meaning Christ—not many ‘offsprings.’ Does the grammar really work that way?"
ot_reference: "Gen 12:7"

ot_text: "Then the LORD appeared to Abram and said, “I will give this land to your offspring.” So Abram built an altar there to the LORD, who had appeared to him."
ot_note: "Cited in Galatians 3:16"
christian_case: "Galatians itself makes the identification explicit: the promised seed is Christ. The strongest Christian defence does not rest on adding or removing an English s. Paul speaks of plural ‘promises,’ reading together Genesis's land, descendants, victory and worldwide blessing themes. On this view, those promises reach their climax in one representative heir, the Messiah. Galatians 3:29 then includes everyone who belongs to Christ as Abraham's seed. The singular and collective senses work together: Christ is the representative one through whom the many inherit. This resembles ancient Jewish ways of rereading corporate scriptural language through representative people."
critical_case: "In Genesis 12:7, ‘offspring’ means Abraham's descendants collectively. The same singular Hebrew noun is compared with uncountable dust and stars, and the land is promised to a continuing people. A plural form was not required to mean many descendants, so singular spelling alone cannot identify one future person. Galatians 3:16 may also draw on several promise passages rather than quote this verse alone. Paul's argument is more sophisticated than a grammatical mistake: he rereads the whole promise around Christ and then makes believers the collective seed in verse 29. That is coherent Christian canonical theology, but it is not the original referent made explicit by Genesis 12:7."
verdict_label: "Representative fulfilment, not lexical prediction"
verdict: "Paul explicitly identifies Christ as Abraham's representative seed and gathers a collective people in him. Genesis 12:7 itself promises land to Abraham's descendants; its singular collective noun does not uniquely predict Jesus. The result is a substantial NT rereading, not a hidden singular-person clue in Genesis grammar."
